title: Fortune Favours the Bold: An Agent-Based Model Reveals Adaptive Advantages of Overconfidence in War

key_points.claim: Model design: spatial grid of states (agents) with geopolitical boundaries endogenously changing; follows Cederman's earlier protocols (GeoContest).
key_points.evidence_quote: we examined the relative performance of states in competition with each other on a 30×30 spatial grid

key_points.claim: Agent cognition: overconfidence is a bias applied only to self-perception; others see true strength, avoiding trivially primed outcomes. Initial α is log-normal, median 1.
key_points.evidence_quote: A state's own perceived resource level is given by αR, so states with α>1 are overconfident

key_points.claim: Simulation cycle has five synchronous phases: resource extraction, decision, resource allocation across fronts, interaction via logistic conflict success function, structural change (provinces become new states inheriting strategy).
Main result: overconfident strategy predominates despite the null expectation of extinction; robust across grid size, boundaries, polarity, k, and α distribution. Optimum is moderate overconfidence.
key_points.evidence_quote: overconfidence consistently emerges as the predominant strategy in the model

key_points.claim: Mechanism 1, the 'lottery effect': overconfident states enter more wars and so are more likely to include the lucky survivors, and early size advantages compound through positive feedback.
key_points.evidence_quote: effectively “buying more lottery tickets” in the competition for survival

key_points.claim: Mechanism 2, emergent offensive alliances (alliance formation): victims split defences without any coordination among attackers. Defensive alliances cannot emerge without higher-level commitment mechanisms.
key_points.evidence_quote: offensive alliances can emerge spontaneously on their own, whereas defensive alliances cannot

key_points.claim: Mechanism 3, attack threshold: w<0.5 favours underconfident states and a peaceful world. w>0.5 favours overconfident states and a war-prone world.
key_points.evidence_quote: if w>0.5, then overconfident states are favoured—even more than they already were

key_points.claim: War costs limit the advantage of overconfidence. The costs are modelled as a share q of the opponent's committed resources.
key_points.evidence_quote: there are limits on the advantages of overconfidence as the costs of fighting increase

key_points.claim: Limitations: no learning, no secession, zero-sum territorial stakes, no defensive alliances. The authors argue that adding learning would only speed up the results.
key_points.evidence_quote: we do not allow states to learn from their own experience, or from observing others

key_points.claim: Robustness details: 200 runs per condition, terminating after 50 idle steps or when one state is left. Supplementary sweep of median final confidence: mean 1.611, range 1.047–3.091.
key_points.evidence_quote: summary statistics for median confidence factors are: mean = 1.611, standard deviation = 0.467, range 1.047–3.091

reliability_notes: Full text was available. It is a peer-reviewed, open-access PLOS ONE paper from 2011. The model is stylized: geopolitics only, with states as agents, and the authors acknowledge limited realism. Findings are the model's own results, and the empirical validity claims are argued by analogy.
